comment_grading:
Homework 20%
Midterm 10%-40%
Final 40%-70%
The weight of midterm and final are taken such that your own score would be at maximum. Eg if u scored horribly in midterm but got a rlly high score in final then midterm weight will be at 10% and final would count for 70%. 
Usually ppl would use homework to “pull” the total score upwards. 
As Prof. Ivan’s papers may be more challenging, the grading is more lenient (ie lower cutoff). As explicitly stated in the syllabus, top 10% or over 90% total score will be guaranteed an A+, while 70+% total score will be guaranteed an A-range. As of 2526 fall, Prof. Ivan decided to try something experimental, that is beating Deepseek V3.1 in midterm and final would be guaranteed an A.
From the previous cohort (22-23?) he taught, around 80% total score is an A+, and A-range is around 60%. 
Finally, generative AI is permitted in homework, but don’t expect it to be very useful, as the current AI technology has not been developed well enough to carry out consistent and accurate mathematical proofs. If you decided to find AI for assistance, make sure to check the response meticulously so as to ensure there are no logical errors. Although the AI may sometimes give correct answers, it may not be the “best” answer (eg correct approach but too many steps). Personally I found Deepseek and Grok give the most consistent answers. Make sure to enable the advanced thinking modes for the gen AI, or it’ll give logically incorrect responses for sure.

App Design:
App design refers to the process of creating the user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) for mobile applications. 
1. User Research: Before starting the design process, it's essential to understand the target audience and their needs. User research helps in identifying user preferences, behaviors, and pain points.
2. Wireframing and Prototyping: Wireframing involves visualizing the app's layout and structure. It helps in planning the app's navigation and functionality. Prototyping involves building interactive mockups to test and validate design concepts.
3. UI Design: User interface design focuses on creating visually appealing and intuitive interfaces. It involves selecting colors, typography, icons, and other visual elements to create a cohesive, user-friendly design.
4. UX Design: User experience design focuses on enhancing user satisfaction and usability. It involves creating seamless user flows, optimizing interactions, and ensuring the app meets the user's goals.
5. Usability Testing: Usability testing involves evaluating the app's design by observing users' interactions and collecting feedback. It helps identify usability issues and refine the design accordingly.
3D Modeling:
3D modeling is creating a three-dimensional representation of objects or scenes using specialized software. Here are some areas where 3D modeling is widely used:
1. Animation and Visual Effects: 3D modeling is extensively used in the entertainment industry for creating animated films, video games, and visual effects. It involves creating realistic characters, environments, and special effects.
2. Product Design and Prototyping: 3D modeling is used in product design to create virtual prototypes and visualize concepts before manufacturing. It enables designers to test different variations and make necessary modifications efficiently.
3. Architecture and Interior Design: 3D modeling is employed in architecture and interior design to create virtual representations of buildings, interiors, and landscapes. It helps architects and designers visualize and present their ideas to clients.
4. Medical and Scientific Visualization: 3D modeling is used in the medical field to create anatomical models for surgical planning, prosthetics, and medical education. It is also used in scientific research for visualizing complex data and simulations.
5. Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR): 3D modeling plays a crucial role in creating immersive experiences in VR and AR applications. It involves building virtual environments and objects that users can interact with in real time.
By learning about app design and 3D modeling, you can acquire valuable skills that can open up exciting career opportunities in industries like software development, gaming, multimedia, architecture, and more.

comment_workload:
[Warning: A Bit Long]
TERRIBLE and HORRIBLE. That’s my final answer for answering the topic of this post. 
According to USTSPACE, MATH 1014 is rated as having a workload of C. If that rating is accurate, then the workload of this course deserves an F—or even a G—assuming C truly reflects the workload of MATH 1014.
I genuinely believe the professor does not respect students. The assessments consist of:
1) Weekly Assignments  
A student posted one of the weekly assignments on USTSPACE—please refer to their comment. Based on my experience, each assignment takes 6–7 hours per week (if you skim ALL the materials and use GenAI slightly). Without GenAI, it can take more than 10 hours. Yet each assignment is worth only 2%.  
Reading materials are posted just a few days (around 3) before the deadline.  
-Marks are graded in increments of 0.1, meaning every decimal can affect your final grade.
2) Book Reviews ×2  
You must read the books thoroughly to write something meaningful, which takes another 6–7 hours. These often overlap with weekly assignments.  
- Graded with 0.1 mark precision (e.g., 11.2/15), but feedback is vague—just “Great job!” or “Nice work!”  
The grading criteria are unclear—possibly based on subjective impressions.
3–5) Final Deliverables During Exam Week  
- Rough Cut and Timeline
- Video
- Paper
Although the course claims to have no final exam, many students enroll expecting a lighter workload. Ironically, the instructor scheduled a film competition during the exam period, worth 1 mark.
- You must attend for 3 hours during exam week to earn it.  
- Assignments 3–5 are also due during the examination period.
Actually, all of the above is just a piece of cake, as it’s written in the syllabus and the instructor kept reminding us during the add/drop period. So if you chose to stay in the course, you should accept it.
What’s truly terrible is that the professor keeps adding “extra bonus marks” activities and assignments.
“Bonus” Marks That Aren’t Really Bonus  
These were not listed in the syllabus, but became essential for anyone aiming for an A-range grade:
6) Two extra weekly assignments (Syllabus said 10, ended up with 12) → 4 bonus marks
7) Three talks with written feedback → 3 bonus marks  
8) In-class questions (0.5 marks each, but students rarely answered, I guess you can ignore it)  
9) Film competition attendance → 1 mark  
Total “Bonus” Marks: At least 8 marks, added without prior notice.  
One talk was announced via email on the same morning it was held. If you want an A-range grade, these “bonuses” are not optional—they’re compulsory.
Personal Reflections
1) The Darkest Day
When I received the Canvas notification titled *“The First Book Review and Weekly Assignment”*, I cried near Canteen II. I even considered ending my life. That’s a true story—I was overwhelmed with quizzes and felt hopeless. I’m deeply thankful to my friends who supported me. That was my darkest day at HKUST.
2) The Film Competition
During exam week, I attended the film session. When the professor announced that attendees would receive 1 bonus mark, the class cheered. I couldn’t. I felt like a poor soul following the professor’s unreasonable demands. I couldn’t feel happy.  
I don’t understand why HKUST students (myself included) are so marks-oriented. One girl spoke up during (other official) class to challenge the professor—but no one supported her. We all stayed silent, myself included.
I really agree with the comment of teaching in one of the posts of HUMA 1430 -  "Unable to understand students' concerns worries or questions."
Final Advice  
Believe me—you’ll regret enrolling in this course. The fast-moving waitlist was a warning. The course enrollment system is a market. Trust the market mechanism. Save your time. Don’t enroll.

comment_content:

*Spring 2025 update: I took COMP2011, and added a section about it in grading*
Background before the course: knew pascal (outdated dse language), C#, Unity, (some) C++, (some) Python
Didn't take the C-placement test (which allows one to go directly to comp2011 programming with C++) since I want to secure GPA for CS major. Thus, I am here.
Feels more like a programming intro course suited for novices (can't really complain: I was supposed to be in COMP2011):
-Topics (python): operators, if else, while and for loops, enumerable (list, tuple, string), using modulus for sequence, function, slicing (enumerable[x:y:z]), boolean logic (limited to and, or, not), data type, text file handling, finite state, dictionary, class and object, recursion
-Topics (turtle): basic control, application of loop in graphics, handling input (click, drag, key press), using multiple turtle objects, color coding
Topics are taught in a high-level manner. By high-level, I mean more surface-level (how things behave) than in-depth (how computers cause things to behave). I guess it is for good as this approach doesn't scare off those who know less about programming prior.
While CS concepts like finite state, color coding are introduced, most topics are just programming.
I can't say that this course is entirely unrelated to CS though, since the lab projects introduce students to different fields of CS: 
-Fields: digital art, game developing, digital music, and AI
-Projects: "getting started" (circle art), guessing game, sketchbook, fireworks, lava game, music system, robot thinking
The projects do look appealing, I was quite drawn in to the music one that I made some extra functions like modulating the music. On top of that, the projects aren't too tedious to complete.
However, (kinda hot take) the instructions are sometimes too hand-holding, where they gave too much hints for certain tasks (e.g. straight up the pseudocode for the part). This may hinder students from learning the mindset needed when working on the fields.
I think they should add more optional tasks for students to try out, which can put a stronger emphasis on the fields while not making the course too stressful, hence, doing a better job at introducing CS.
That being said, they provide many useful materials, including example codes, interactive examples, and most importantly previous midterms/finals with video explanation, helpful for those with less advanced background to catch up.

-a variety of difficulty: questions can be easy as writing a line of code from giving instructions (e.g. assigning variable to a list), to hard as handling recursion for art with obfuscated variables, fairer than just being plain easy or plain hard
-better than previous exams: questions are more focused on logic than before with less blatant careless checks (= in if statement, missing quotation mark, typo), and the final doesn't have those straight up maths questions for this sem
-chiller competition than I expected (at least for a+): the pastpapers of 2022 and 2023 were quite easy, which made me think that not getting full mark might actually cost an a+. However, the final turns out to be harder this sem, with some questions being actually challenging than just having every questions easy. As mentioned, only ~0.57% of all students got full marks, implying that a+ competition is not too fierce this sem. This is why I gave B instead of C for this category. May reconsider the grading if I know more about the cutoff
Some advice:
-Grind pastpapers, they are available on the course website and some questions are straight up borrowed from them
-Complete all labs, even non-handin ones, as they can use all lab projects in questions. Make sure that you are familiar with the labs
-Careless mistakes will be your greatest enemy, while the competition is less fierce, don't let it destroy your subgrade
-Risky if you don't have time: paste the code in the question and run it using your answer if you can directly test that code, it may just be my anxiety that makes me do that
COMP2011 update:
I am aware that this course is being rebranded to COMP1023, but if you saw this, here is my recommendation whether to take the C-placement test and waiver COMP1023 or not.
*If COMP1023 is taught by Desmond Tsoi, which is likely, please do not (2024 intakes may have 1 less course, which is apparently COMP2012, with him for this, very sad)*
Otherwise, here is a few points to consider, take it with a grain of salt, as I don't know how different COMP1023 will be from COMP1021.
COMP2011 is not only about programming, but also how C++ works. It is also taught in a lower level, i.e. memory allocation, dynamic memory, etc. Just being good at programming is not enough, but you also need to actively learn C++'s inner workings if you haven't.
If your programming background is not deep enough, it is recommended that you don't waiver COMP1023.
As for grading, COMP2011's takers are very polarized: there are 2 peaks in the final's stats, one at 21-30 and one at 71-80 (out of 100). Even if "criterion-referencing" is used, it is not hard for those with a background in programming to fall in the "10-25% A-range" (ARO, 2025). Not to flex but for me, COMP2011 is an easy A+.
Since 2025 intake is department-based, it is likely that you don't need to join the best24 GPA race for CSE. If you want 3 credits for other courses (help me check if waivering COMP1023 doesn't get its credit transferred or not), or simply don't want to introduce yourself to programming again, go ahead for COMP2011. comment_content: This course offers a broad perspective on technology and innovation, making it interesting and useful, especially if you're here for fun. It includes real-life examples of how companies like Apple, Google, and Amazon promote themselves in different ways, and you'll analyze the internal policies of these successful companies. However, if you're aiming for a good grade and are probably an engineering student, you might want to consider other SSC courses.
comment_teaching: The slides are quite simple and clean, and the professor leaves plenty of time for questions and discussions, making the class very interactive and easy to catch up with. He teaches very well and understands how to make the material interesting. Although I don't want to exaggerate, his class is one of the few where I don't fall asleep during the lecture.
comment_grading:

The gradings are reasonable. I received around mean in everything and received B+
comment_workload:
The workload for this course is pretty low, making it fair enough for a common core class. 
There is a group project where you write a report analyzing a disruptive technology or company, and you also need to write a similar report on your own. While the workload can be high at the end of the semester, my groupmates were very tolerant and willing to guide me as the only year 1 student in the group, and we ended up with a good project grade.

comment_content:
You will learn the basics of calculus in this course if you haven't taken M1/M2 in secondary school, which teaches you almost all the basics from differentiation to limits to integration, etc.
There is a lot of content that is covered by this course as it's 2-3 years of M1/M2 dse covered in just 1 semester, it would be better if they made it a year-long course or something...
comment_teaching: The instructor, prof Lam, went through the content, writing each chapter's concepts with very few example questions without the use of a PowerPoint, sometimes leaving you more confused than before you entered the lecture hall.
comment_grading: I would say the grading of the course is meh, not too bad nor too good. However, it sucked when I found out there were a lot of people in the course who took M1/M2 in their secondary school but they dropped it later in form 5/6, which feels a bit unfair to the students who has 0 knowledge of calculus. as that pulled the distribution curve higher.
comment_workload:
Just doing the webwork homework alone isn't enough revision for this course. 
It's better to take the lecture time to do a self-revision of the chapters and do the sample questions from the textbook than to attend the boring 2-hour lecture, as you will most likely learn 100 times more effectively.
I also highly recommend online resources like watching Organic Chemistry Tutor or those hkdse m1/m2 videos on YouTube.

comment_content:
The course covers some of python's basic programming language based on turtle, which is a little too easy for college students.
In the lab class, the given files usually include some codes which are not taught in the lecture class. This means if you want to get yourself fully understand the whole code, you need to pay more effort on the "extracurricular content".
comment_teaching: The teaching process is very slow and ensures that everyone understands it.
comment_grading:
Grades depend on your relative ranking. You can refer to materials in the exams.
The test should measure how well students grasp and apply the knowledge, not how well they remember the examples in the content. However, our final exam this term was very unfriendly, which includes lots of examples from the class and the rules of the lab class. We were very shocked when we see the question and felt uneasy to check the slides containing the answer. Almost every student in this course I know was complaining about it after the final exam.
comment_workload: If you have learned something about Python or programing, the workload will be low to you.
